mainTopic: Two men with the same name and their loan notes, unclear receipts and statements about repaid notes, and the start of the משנה about a ערב.
overview: This amud continues the case of two men in one town who are both named יוסף בן שמעון. First the גמרא explains why a ברייתא says they cannot collect a שטר חוב even from other people. One answer is that they disagree whether a note's rights pass by handing it over (אותיות נקנות במסירה). The other answer is that everyone agrees it passes, and they disagree whether the holder must prove it was given to him. That second answer leads to the dispute between אביי and רבא, each reading a ברייתא about brothers in his own way. Next, a second ברייתא lets the two men collect from each other, and the גמרא ties this to whether a note may be written for a borrower without the lender present. The גמרא then works through the משנה's case of a receipt that just says 'יוסף בן שמעון' and the advice to write more generations of names. A new משנה follows about a father who does not know which of his notes was repaid. רבא and רבינא then establish that unclear wording goes against the holder of the document. The amud ends by opening a new משנה about a loan made through a ערב.

steps.title: A ברייתא says they cannot collect from others either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that seems to contradict the משנה's implication, and asks what the two sources disagree about.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about the ברייתא that teaches: just as the two יוסף בן שמעון cannot produce a שטר חוב against each other, so too they cannot produce one against other people. What are they arguing about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to clash with what we learned from the משנה. It asks what the underlying disagreement is, and this sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the משנה we learned that a יוסף בן שמעון may collect from outsiders. The ברייתא says he may not. Instead of rejecting one source, the גמרא asks what idea each side holds that leads to its ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: A promissory note, a written record of a loan
They produce (a document in court to collect)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. 'זה על זה' means the two יוסף בן שמעון against each other. 'על אחרים' means one of them collecting from some other borrower.

phrases.english: But that which is taught in a baraita:
Just as they cannot produce
a promissory note, this one against that one —
phrases.notes: 'This one against that one' means the two men with the same name, יוסף בן שמעון.

phrases.english: so too they cannot produce one against others,
about what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a ברייתא that contradicts the inference from the משנה discussed earlier on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference from the משנה that a יוסף בן שמעון may collect from others
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly says they cannot collect from others, so the two sources seem to conflict.

steps.title: They disagree about transferring a debt by handing over the note
steps.stepSummary: First answer: the משנה holds that a שטר חוב can be transferred by simply handing it over, and the ברייתא holds that it cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about whether the 'letters' (the right to collect written in the note) are acquired by handing over the note. Our תנא says yes, they are. The תנא of the ברייתא says no, they are not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the contradiction by pointing to a basic disagreement: can you give someone a debt just by handing him the שטר חוב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If handing over the note works, the other יוסף בן שמעון might have received it legitimately from his namesake, so he may collect, as the משנה implies. If handing over does not work, he could never hold the note legally, so he cannot collect, as the ברייתא says.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'letters': the written content of a document, the right to collect the debt
Our תנא, the one of our משנה
The 'outside' תנא, the one of the ברייתא

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether a debt can be sold or transferred just by giving over the שטר is a major topic in the laws of acquisition.

phrases.english: They disagree about whether letters are acquired by handing over —
phrases.notes: 'Letters' means what is written in the note, which is really the right to collect the loan.

phrases.english: The tanna of our mishna holds:
letters are acquired by handing over;
and the tanna of the baraita holds:
letters are not acquired by handing over.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1 by identifying the principle in dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מחלוקת תנאים: the two sources reflect two opinions on a basic principle
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and ברייתא seem to contradict each other with no explanation.
steps.terutzMaskana: They disagree about whether a debt is transferred by handing over the שטר חוב.

steps.title: Or: everyone agrees, and they disagree about needing proof
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: both agree that handing over the note transfers the debt. They disagree about whether the holder must prove the note was really given to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: everyone agrees that letters are acquired by handing over. The disagreement is about bringing proof. Our תנא says the holder does not need to bring proof. The תנא of the ברייתא says he does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to explain the disagreement, one that keeps both sources agreeing on the basic rule of transfer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the question is not whether a transfer can work but whether we assume it happened. The משנה trusts the holder without proof, so he collects. The ברייתא requires proof that the other יוסף בן שמעון gave it to him to collect, and without that proof he cannot collect.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces an alternative answer

steps.whatToRemember: Two ways to explain the dispute: (1) whether handing over a שטר transfers the debt at all, or (2) everyone agrees it does, and the argument is whether the holder must prove he received it legitimately.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
that everyone agrees —
letters are acquired by handing over,
and here, about needing to bring proof
phrases.notes: Proof that the note was handed to him to collect, not just left with him or found.

phrases.english: they disagree —
The tanna of our mishna holds:
he does not need to bring proof,
and the tanna of the baraita holds:
he needs to bring proof —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to step 1 that removes the disagreement over אותיות נקנות במסירה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative explanation: shared principle, different evidentiary requirement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute must be about whether handing over a שטר transfers the debt.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both agree that handing over works. They disagree only about whether the holder must prove the transfer happened.

steps.title: The known dispute: must the new holder prove he received the note?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites the dispute between אביי and רבא that stands behind the second answer. Both agree that a note's rights transfer by handing it over. They argue about whether the holder must bring proof that it was really given to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: the rights in a written document are acquired by handing it over. אביי says the holder must bring proof. רבא says he does not need to bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up the second answer from step 3 by pointing to an already-known argument between אביי and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 said the two sources argue about whether the holder needs proof. This step shows that this exact argument already exists. Both אביי and רבא accept that handing over transfers the debt. The only question is whether holding the note is enough evidence that it was given, or whether the holder must prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'letters'. Here it means the rights written in a document, such as a שטר חוב.
Are acquired by handing over the document.

phrases.english: As it was stated: letters are acquired by handing over [the document];
Abaye says: he must bring proof,
phrases.notes: Proof that the original lender really gave him the note. He might otherwise have just picked it up.

phrases.aramaic: וְרָבָא אָמַר: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְהָבִיא רְאָיָה.
phrases.english: and Rava says: he does not need to bring proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Grounds the second answer of step 3 in an existing dispute between אמוראים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone agrees that אותיות נקנות במסירה. אביי requires the holder to prove he received the note, and רבא does not.

steps.title: אביי's proof from a brother holding the father's note
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a ברייתא: a brother who holds a note from the estate must bring proof. He argues that the same rule should apply to anyone holding a note.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: How do I know my view? It was taught in a ברייתא: if one of the brothers has a שטר חוב coming out from under his hand, he must bring proof. Doesn't the same apply to others?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tries to prove from a ברייתא that whoever holds a note must prove it was really given to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, a brother holds a note owed to their late father and wants to collect it for himself. The ברייתא says he must prove that it was given to him. אביי reasons that brothers are just one example, so anyone holding someone else's note should need proof.

keyTerms.meaning: 'From where do I say it?' An אמורא uses this to introduce his source.
Literally 'coming out from under his hand'. It means the note is found in his possession.

phrases.english: Abaye said: From where do I say it?
As it was taught: one of the brothers
who has a promissory note in his possession,
it is upon him to bring proof.
What, is it not the same law for others?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי supports his side of the dispute from step 4.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's view that a holder of a transferred note must bring proof.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about one of the brothers holding a שטר חוב, who must bring proof.

steps.title: רבא: brothers are a special case
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the proof. Brothers tend to grab items from the shared estate, so they need proof. That does not mean other people do.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: Brothers are different, because they grab from one another.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes away אביי's proof by saying the ברייתא is only talking about a special situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Brothers live close together and share an estate, so a brother may simply have taken the note from the family's things. That is why the ברייתא asks him for proof. A stranger holding a note does not raise the same suspicion, so the rule cannot be extended to others.

phrases.english: And Rava said: brothers are different,
since they grab from one another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof from step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects stretching the ברייתא's rule beyond brothers.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Brothers are suspected of taking items from the estate, so the need for proof comes from that suspicion and not from a general rule.

steps.title: Another version: רבא proves his view from the same ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רבא himself quotes the ברייתא as a proof. Only brothers need proof because they grab from each other, so others do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רבא said: How do I know my view? It was taught: if one of the brothers has a שטר חוב in his possession, he must bring proof. It is brothers who grab from each other, but others do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the exchange. Here רבא uses the same ברייתא to support his own side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the ברייתא was אביי's proof and רבא only deflected it. In this version, the ברייתא's choice to mention brothers shows that the proof requirement is limited to them. So other holders of a note need no proof.
steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees that handing over a note transfers it. אביי requires the holder to prove he received it, and רבא does not. The ברייתא about brothers is read by אביי as a general rule, and by רבא as a special case because brothers grab from each other.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions quote the same ברייתא. The only difference is who uses it as a proof. In the first version it is אביי's proof and רבא pushes it aside. In the second version it is רבא's own proof.

phrases.english: There are those who say: Rava said:
From where do I say it?
As it was taught: one of the brothers
who has a promissory note in his possession,
it is upon him to bring proof.
It is brothers who grab from one another,
but others do not.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רָבָא: מְנָא אָמֵינָא לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Retells steps 5 and 6 in another version, where the ברייתא supports רבא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that a holder of a transferred note does not need proof.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about brothers. Mentioning brothers specifically implies that others are not required to bring proof.

steps.title: אביי explains why the ברייתא mentions brothers
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the ברייתא mentions brothers only to block a mistaken idea. One might think brothers watch each other so closely that a brother holding a note needs no proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אביי? He would say the ברייתא needed to mention brothers. You might have thought: since brothers grab from each other, they are careful to guard against it, so a brother holding a note does not need proof. The ברייתא teaches us that he still does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how אביי answers רבא's proof from the ברייתא about brothers. אביי says brothers are not a special case. The ברייתא names them only so we don't think they are exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא read the ברייתא as saying 'only brothers need proof.' אביי turns it around. Because brothers grab from each other, each one guards the estate closely, so you might think any note a brother holds must be legitimately his. The ברייתא teaches that even brothers need proof, and certainly everyone else does.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary for it (the ברייתא) to say this
It could enter your mind to say (a mistaken idea the source wants to block)

steps.confusionAlert: The same fact, that brothers grab from each other, leads in opposite directions. For רבא it is a reason why brothers need proof. For אביי it is a reason why you might have thought they DON'T need proof.

phrases.english: And Abaye? It was necessary for it to mention brothers,
since it could enter your mind to say:
since they grab from one another,
say that they are very careful,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the letter in round brackets. Either way, it means each brother watches the others closely.

phrases.english: and they do not need to bring proof;
it teaches us that they do.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends אביי against רבא's proof in Step 7 by rereading why the ברייתא names brothers.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains a detail in the source (צריכותא): the case is named to block a mistaken idea, not to exclude others.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Brothers guard each other closely, so a note held by a brother might be presumed legitimately his without proof.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even brothers must bring proof, and so must anyone else holding a note.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבא's inference that the ברייתא's mention of brothers excludes everyone else.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא names brothers only to block the mistaken idea that they guard each other so closely that a brother needs no proof (מיזדהר זהירי). It is not limiting the rule to brothers.

steps.title: A ברייתא lets the two יוסף בן שמעון collect from each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the two men named יוסף בן שמעון. It quotes a ברייתא that lets them collect notes from each other, and asks what that disagreement depends on.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about the ברייתא that teaches: just as they can collect a שטר חוב from other people, so they can collect from each other? What are they arguing about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the main case of the משנה, two men with the same name. It brings a ברייתא that disagrees with the משנה and asks what the root of the argument is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה says two men named יוסף בן שמעון cannot collect a note from each other. This ברייתא says they can. The גמרא wants the underlying reason that splits the two views.

keyTerms.meaning: But what about that which is taught in a ברייתא
Produce a note in court to collect

phrases.english: But what about that which is taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁמּוֹצִיאִין הֵן שְׁטַר חוֹב עַל אֲחֵרִים –
phrases.english: just as they can produce a promissory note against others,
phrases.notes: "They" are the two men in the same town who are both named יוסף בן שמעון.

phrases.english: so can they produce notes against one another;
about what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אביי/רבא side discussion and returns to the case of the two יוסף בן שמעון.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides our משנה from the ברייתא that lets them collect from each other.

steps.title: They argue about writing a note without the lender present
steps.stepSummary: The argument depends on one question: may a scribe write a loan note for a borrower when the lender is not there?
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about whether a scribe may write a note for a borrower even when the lender is not with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question in one line: the dispute depends on whether a note may be written for the borrower alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a scribe may write a note without the lender present, a note naming the same person as borrower and lender can be misused. If the scribe may not, the risk disappears. The next step spells out how this works.

keyTerms.meaning: We write a note for the borrower

phrases.english: About whether we write a note for a borrower

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מַלְוֶה עִמּוֹ קָמִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: even if the lender is not with him, they disagree.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּכוֹתְבִין שְׁטָר לַלֹּוֶה וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מַלְוֶה עִמּוֹ קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two sources disagree about whether a note may be written for a borrower without the lender present.

steps.title: How the trick works under our משנה's view
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה holds that a note may be written for the borrower alone. So one יוסף בן שמעון could have a note written as if he were borrowing from the other, then turn around and claim the other owes him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא of our משנה holds that a scribe may write a note for a borrower even without the lender there. So sometimes one of them goes to a scribe and witnesses and says, 'Write me a note, because I want to borrow from my friend יוסף בן שמעון.' After they write and sign it, he keeps it and tells the other, 'Give me the hundred you borrowed from me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the danger our משנה is worried about. That danger is why the משנה does not let the two men collect from each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both men have the same name, a note saying 'יוסף בן שמעון borrowed from יוסף בן שמעון' cannot show which one is the lender. Because a note can be written with only the borrower present, one of them could get a note written and then pretend he was the lender. So our משנה stops them from collecting such notes from each other.
steps.whatToRemember: Our משנה lets a note be written for the borrower alone. With two people of the same name, that could let one of them fake being the lender. That is why the משנה does not let them collect from each other.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the ruling about same-name people depends on a broader rule about how loan notes are written.

phrases.english: The tanna of our Mishnah holds:
we may write a note for a borrower,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מַלְוֶה עִמּוֹ;
phrases.english: even if the lender is not with him;
sometimes one goes to a scribe and witnesses,
and says to them: Write a note for me,

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָעֵינַן לְמֵיזַף מִיּוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן חַבְרַי;
phrases.english: as I want to borrow from my fellow Yosef ben Shimon;
and after they write it and sign it for him,
he holds onto it and says to the other:
Give me the hundred that you borrowed from me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out how the principle in Step 10 leads to our משנה's ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because a note may be written with only the borrower present, a same-name person could fake being the lender. So our משנה does not let them collect from each other.

steps.title: The other ברייתא holds a note needs the lender present
steps.stepSummary: The תנא of the ברייתא holds that a note is written for a borrower only when the lender is with him, so there is no fear of a fake note between the two יוסף בן שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא of the outside ברייתא holds: we do not write a note for the borrower unless the lender is with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the answer from step 10. It explains the other side, the ברייתא that lets the two יוסף בן שמעון collect from each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a note can be written only when the lender is present, a note between the two men is real, because the lender agreed to it. So there is no worry that one wrote a fake note against the other, and they may collect from each other.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא of the outside teaching, meaning the ברייתא, not our משנה

steps.whatToRemember: The whole disagreement comes down to one rule. Our משנה says a note may be written for the borrower alone, so they cannot collect from each other. The ברייתא says the lender must be present, so they can.

phrases.english: The tanna of the outside [baraita] holds:
phrases.notes: He means the ברייתא from step 9, which let the two יוסף בן שמעון collect notes from each other.

phrases.english: we do not write a note for the borrower
unless the lender is with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided answer begun in step 11, which gave our משנה's side
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא holds that a note needs the lender present, so a note between the two men is real and can be collected

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about a found receipt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה. If a paper saying 'the note of יוסף בן שמעון is repaid' is found among a lender's papers, the notes of both men are treated as repaid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone found among his papers a note saying 'The note of יוסף בן שמעון is repaid,' the notes of both of them are repaid, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה to set up a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lender holds notes against both men named יוסף בן שמעון. He finds a paper saying one note was paid, but it does not say which one. Since we cannot tell, both notes are treated as paid.

phrases.english: If it was found for someone among his documents:
"The note of Yosef ben Shimon is repaid"
the notes of both of them are repaid, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A receipt for 'יוסף בן שמעון' that does not say which one cancels both notes

steps.title: Contradiction with the משנה's earlier line
steps.stepSummary: The משנה implies that without the found receipt, the lender could collect from one יוסף בן שמעון. But the משנה said earlier that no one can collect a note against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that it was found. So if it was not found, he could take out a note and collect? But we learned: 'Nor can someone else take out a loan note against them'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads an implication into the משנה and shows that it clashes with an earlier line of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'it was found' suggest that the receipt is the only problem, and that the lender could otherwise collect. But earlier the משנה ruled that an outsider cannot collect from either man, since each can say 'the note isn't against me.' The two lines seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is that, an opening for an inference
He can take out (a note to collect)
But we learned! (an opening for a contradiction)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not on the found receipt itself. It is on what the משנה implies would happen without the receipt.

phrases.english: The reason is that it was found;
but if it was not found, he could take out [a note and collect];
but didn't we learn: "Nor can another
take out a loan note against them"!
phrases.notes: This is the earlier line of our משנה, about an outsider holding a note against 'יוסף בן שמעון.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the line just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's implied ruling that without the found receipt the lender could collect
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier line says no one can collect from either יוסף בן שמעון, which contradicts the implication

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: the notes have the grandfather's name
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that the lender's notes have the names written in full, with the grandfather's name, so normally he would know whom to collect from.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: this is talking about names that are 'tripled.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the contradiction by describing a different kind of note.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here each note names the man, his father and his grandfather, so it is clear who owes what. The earlier rule, that no one can collect, is about notes with only two names. So the two lines talk about different cases and do not contradict.

keyTerms.meaning: Tripled, meaning the name, the father's name and the grandfather's name are all written

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
With tripled [names].
phrases.notes: Tripled means the grandfather's name is also written, so the two men can be told apart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different case: the names are written in full
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines talk about the same kind of note, so they contradict
steps.terutzMaskana: The receipt case involves notes with full names, so without a receipt he could collect

steps.title: Why not check whose name is on the receipt?
steps.stepSummary: If the names are written in full, just look at the receipt and see which יוסף בן שמעון it names.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us look at the receipt and see in whose name it is written!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ירמיה's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If full names are used, the receipt should also carry a full name. Then we would know which note was paid, and both should not be cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt, literally 'a breaking' of the debt

phrases.english: But let us look at the receipt:
in whose name it is written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי ירמיה's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's case of tripled names
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With full names, the receipt would show which man paid, so there would be no doubt

steps.title: רב הושעיא: full names on the notes, not on the receipt
steps.stepSummary: רב הושעיא says the notes had full names, but the receipt did not, so we cannot tell which debt it refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הושעיא said: the names are tripled in the loan note, but not tripled in the receipt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הושעיא defends רבי ירמיה's answer by sharpening the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The loan notes clearly separate the two men, so the lender could normally collect from each. But the receipt says only 'יוסף בן שמעון,' so we do not know which note it cancels. That is why both notes count as repaid.

keyTerms.meaning: Receipt, the Hebrew word for תברא

steps.whatToRemember: In רבי ירמיה's approach, as sharpened by רב הושעיא: the notes have full names, so collecting is normally possible. The receipt has only a short name, so it creates doubt and cancels both notes. Step 18 gives אביי's different answer.

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya said:
Where [the names] are tripled in the note,
but they are not tripled in the receipt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 16
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Full names would appear on the receipt too, so there is no doubt
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the notes have full names, and the short name on the receipt causes the doubt

steps.title: אביי: The receipt was found among the borrower's papers
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers the question from step 14 in a different way. He says the משנה is talking about a borrower who owes money to two men named יוסף בן שמעון. A receipt among the borrower's own papers says the note of 'יוסף בן שמעון' is repaid, so both men's notes are treated as repaid.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This is what the משנה means. If a paper is found among the borrower's documents saying, 'The note of יוסף בן שמעון against me is repaid,' then the notes of both of them are treated as repaid.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a second answer to the question from step 14. He reads the משנה as talking about the borrower's papers, not the lender's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 asked how anyone could collect from a יוסף בן שמעון if the משנה already said no one can. אביי avoids that problem: here the two men named יוסף בן שמעון are the lenders, and one borrower owes both of them. Since the receipt does not say which יוסף בן שמעון was paid, neither of them can collect.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means. Used to reread an earlier text.
The notes of both of them are treated as repaid

steps.confusionAlert: In אביי's reading, the two men named יוסף בן שמעון are the LENDERS, not the borrowers. One borrower owes money to both of them.

phrases.english: Abaye said: This is what it is saying:
If there is found by the borrower, among his documents,

phrases.aramaic: ״שְׁטָרוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן עָלַי, פָּרוּעַ״
phrases.english: "The note of Yosef ben Shimon against me is repaid"
the notes of both of them are treated as repaid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the question in step 14, in place of the approach of רבי ירמיה and רב הושעיא (steps 15-17).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the case: the receipt belongs to the borrower, and the same-named men are the lenders.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The receipt was found among the lender's papers, so it seemed the lender could have collected from a יוסף בן שמעון.
steps.terutzMaskana: The receipt was found among the borrower's papers. Neither lender named יוסף בן שמעון can collect, because we cannot tell which one was paid.

steps.title: If both men are priests, they write more generations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: two people with the same name should write three generations of their names. A ברייתא adds that if both of them are כהנים, they should keep writing more generations until the names are different.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: What should they do? They should write three generations, and so on. A ברייתא taught: If both of them were כהנים, they should write more generations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's advice for two people with the same name. It then adds a ברייתא that covers a case the משנה did not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's fallback was to write that one of them is a כהן. That does not help if both are כהנים. The ברייתא says that in that case they keep listing ancestors until the names differ.

keyTerms.meaning: They should 'triple', meaning write three generations: the man, his father, and his grandfather

phrases.english: How should they act?
They should triple, etc.
phrases.notes: "Etc." means the rest of the משנה line, which says that if needed they write that one of them is a כהן.

phrases.english: It was taught: If both of them were priests,
they should write generations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the משנה, about how to tell two same-named people apart.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If both same-named people are כהנים, they list more generations of ancestors to tell them apart.

steps.title: New משנה: A father says one of his notes is repaid
steps.stepSummary: A father tells his son that one of his notes is repaid, but he does not know which one. All the notes are then treated as repaid. If two of the notes are from the same borrower, the larger one is treated as repaid and the smaller one is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone says to his son, 'One note among my notes is repaid, and I do not know which one.' All the notes are treated as repaid. If two notes are found there from one person, the larger one is repaid and the smaller one is not repaid.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with a lender who knows one of his notes was paid but cannot remember which.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since any note might be the paid one, no single note can be collected, so all are treated as repaid. But if one borrower has two notes, the משנה limits the doubt to that borrower: we treat the larger note as the paid one, and the smaller note can still be collected.

keyTerms.meaning: And I do not know which one it is
The larger one (the note for more money)
The smaller one (the note for less money)

steps.whatToRemember: An unknown repaid note makes every note doubtful, so all are treated as repaid. When two notes are from one borrower, the larger is treated as repaid.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who says to his son:
"A note among my notes is repaid,
and I do not know which one it is"
all the notes are treated as repaid.
If two notes from one person were found there,
the larger one is repaid,
and the smaller one is not repaid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה on a related subject: a receipt or statement that does not say which debt was paid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If it is unknown which note was repaid, all are treated as repaid. If two notes are from one borrower, the larger is treated as repaid and the smaller is not.

steps.title: רבא: Saying 'a note' versus saying 'a debt'
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that the lender's exact words matter. If he tells the borrower, 'A note of yours in my hand is repaid,' only one note is treated as repaid: the larger one. If he says, 'A debt of yours in my hand is repaid,' all the notes are treated as repaid.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבא said: If a lender says, 'A note of yours in my hand is repaid,' the larger one is repaid and the smaller one is not. If he says, 'A debt of yours in my hand is repaid,' all the notes are repaid.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a case to the משנה about one borrower with two notes. He shows that the wording of the lender's statement changes the result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'note' points to a single document, so only one note is treated as repaid, and we choose the larger. The word 'debt' covers everything the borrower owes as one whole, so all the notes are treated as repaid.

keyTerms.meaning: A note of yours that is in my hand
A debt of yours that is in my hand

steps.whatToRemember: 'שטר' (a note) means only one note is repaid, the larger one. 'חוב' (a debt) means all the notes are repaid.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that in money matters, the exact word a person uses can decide how much of a debt is cancelled.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rava says:
"A note of yours in my hand is repaid":
the larger one is repaid and the smaller one is not repaid.
"A debt of yours in my hand is repaid":
all the notes are treated as repaid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רבא שטר לך בידי פרוע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's case of two notes from one borrower by focusing on how the lender words his statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'A note of yours is repaid' cancels only the larger note. 'A debt of yours is repaid' cancels all the notes.

steps.title: Would the same rule apply to selling a field?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רבא: if unclear wording is read against the speaker, then a seller who says 'my field is sold to you' should lose his larger field. And if he says 'a field that I have is sold to you,' should he lose all of his fields?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רבא: But if that is true, then if someone says 'My field is sold to you,' is the larger field sold to him? And if he says 'A field that I have is sold to you,' are all of his fields sold to him?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges רבא's rule from step 21. He applies the same thinking to a sale of land and gets a result that sounds wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21, the lender's unclear words were read in the way that hurt him: the larger note, or all the notes, were treated as repaid. רבינא says that by the same logic, a seller's unclear words should also be read against him. Then the buyer would get the bigger field, or even every field, which seems unreasonable.

keyTerms.meaning: But if that is so (an opening that pushes a rule to a result that seems wrong)
My field is sold to you

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rava:
But if that is so,
"My field is sold to you"
is the larger field sold to him?
"A field that I have is sold to you"
are all of his fields sold to him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרָבָא: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's rule from step 21 by applying it to a sale.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that the lender's unclear wording is read against him (the larger note, or all the notes, count as repaid)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If unclear words are always read against the speaker, a seller's unclear words would hand the buyer the larger field, or all his fields. That result seems wrong.

steps.title: The person holding the document is at the disadvantage
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that in a sale, the buyer holds the document, so he gets the smaller amount. The real rule is that whoever holds the document is at the disadvantage. With the notes, that person is the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the person holding the document has the lower hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רבינא. The rule was never 'go against the speaker.' It is 'go against the one holding the document.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a sale, the buyer holds the document and wants to take more from the seller, so he gets only the smaller amount. In the case of the notes, the lender holds the documents and wants to collect more, so he is the one who loses. Both cases follow one rule.

keyTerms.meaning: There (in the case being asked about)
He has the lower hand; he is at the disadvantage

steps.whatToRemember: When the wording of a document is unclear, the person holding the document is at the disadvantage. A buyer gets the smaller amount, and a lender loses the larger note or all the notes.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a general rule for reading any unclear document. It works the same way for loans and for sales.

phrases.english: There,
phrases.notes: He means the case of selling a field.

phrases.english: the holder of the document has the lower hand.
phrases.notes: In a sale, the buyer holds the document, so he gets the smaller amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם, יַד בַּעַל הַשְּׁטָר עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Restates the rule in a sharper way that fits both cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule seemed to be that unclear words always go against the speaker. That would make a seller lose his larger field, or all of his fields.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule goes against whoever holds the document. In a sale that is the buyer, so he gets less. With the notes that is the lender, so he loses more.

steps.title: New משנה: a loan made with a guarantor
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה begins: someone who lends money to another person through a ערב (guarantor) may not collect the debt from the guarantor.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who lends money to his friend through a guarantor may not collect from the guarantor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new משנה on a new topic: a loan that has a ערב (guarantor). This opening line starts a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ערב is a person who backs up someone else's loan. The משנה's first rule is that the lender may not collect from the ערב. The rest of the discussion will build on this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantor who backs up someone else's loan

phrases.english: Mishnah:

phrases.aramaic: הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ עַל יְדֵי עָרֵב,
phrases.english: One who lends to his fellow through a guarantor
may not collect from the guarantor.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ עַל יְדֵי עָרֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion of unclear documents and opens a new משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender who lent through a guarantor may not collect the debt from the guarantor.
